title: The Apostolic Fathers
lead: The Apostolic Fathers is the name scholars give to a small group of Christian writings from the generation or two after the apostles, roughly AD 90 to 160: letters, a church manual, sermons, a martyr's story and a book of visions. They are not in the New Testament of the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican or Protestant churches (each book's page gives the sources, and notes where a church once counted one of them), and they show how the churches after the apostles believed, prayed, read Scripture and ordered their life.

sections.b: The collection has no fixed list. Kirsopp Lake's Loeb edition (1912–1913), the base text of this site, prints in volume 1 the letter of the Roman church to Corinth called 1 Clement, the sermon called 2 Clement, the Letters of Ignatius, Polycarp to the Philippians, the Didache and the Epistle of Barnabas, and in volume 2 the Shepherd of Hermas, the Martyrdom of Polycarp and the letter to Diognetus. The site translates fifteen of them: the Didache, the Epistle of Barnabas, 1 Clement, 2 Clement, all seven letters of Ignatius (to the Ephesians, the Magnesians, the Trallians, the Romans, the Philadelphians, the Smyrnaeans and Polycarp), Polycarp to the Philippians, the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the Shepherd of Hermas and the Epistle to Diognetus.

sections.b: These writings stand between the New Testament and the great church writers of the late second century. They quote or echo several New Testament books (1 Clement names Paul's first letter to Corinth, 47:1), and they show the questions of their day: how the Law of Moses applies to Christians (Barnabas), how a church should be led and what happens when it removes its leaders (1 Clement 40–44), how to baptize, fast and give thanks at the meal (Didache 7–10), how to face death for the faith (Martyrdom of Polycarp). The churches read what they say about the ministry differently: 1 Clement's page gives a Catholic and an Anglican reading of chapters 40–44, and the site's cards at Acts 14 and 1 Timothy 3 set out the wider debate.
sections.refs: 1 Clement 42:1–44:6; Didache 7:1–10:7; Barnabas 2:1–3:6; Martyrdom of Polycarp 9:1–3

sections.h: At the edge of the canon
sections.b: Some of these writings came close to the Bible. The Epistle of Barnabas follows Revelation in Codex Sinaiticus of the fourth century, with the Shepherd of Hermas after it (Lake; Ladeuze), and Clement of Alexandria quotes it as the work of "the Apostle Barnabas" (Stromata 2.6). The two letters under Clement's name follow the New Testament in Codex Alexandrinus of the fifth century, and the list in the last of the Apostolic Canons names "Two Epistles of Clemens" among "our own books, that is, those of the New Testament," after Jude and before Acts (canon 85), a list Westcott judged "of no value" as evidence and probably of the sixth century. Eusebius took Dionysius of Corinth's letter of about AD 170 to show "that it had been the custom from the beginning" to read 1 Clement in the church there (Church History 4.23.11). But Eusebius put Barnabas, the Shepherd and "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the spurious books (3.25.4), and Athanasius, while closing the New Testament at 27 books, set apart other books, "not indeed included in the Canon," to be read by new believers: the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, "that which is called the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Shepherd" (Festal Letter 39). The topic How Books Got into the Bible tells the wider story.

A long letter of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth, dated by Lake between AD 75 and 110, with "a general agreement among critics" for the last decade of the first century, and credited by tradition to Clement of Rome. It answers a revolt in which some Corinthians had removed their elders, and argues from order in the creation, the army, the body and the Temple that the ministry set up by the apostles must be respected (40–44). It contains an early account of the deaths of Peter and Paul (5) and a great prayer for the church and the rulers (59–61). See the topic Clement of Rome.

An anonymous treatise that Lake dates to "the end of the first or beginning of the second century." Ladeuze argued that it was written at Alexandria; Lake says only that it was meant for readers among whom "Alexandrian ideas prevailed," and that its place cannot be fixed. It reads the sacrifices, fasts, circumcision, food laws, Sabbath and Temple as figures of Christ and the church, and claims that Israel lost the covenant at Sinai (4:6–8; 14:1–4), a claim that conflicts with Romans 9:4–5 and 11:28–29. It ends with the Two Ways of light and darkness (18–20), close to the opening of the Didache.
sections.refs: Barnabas 4:6–8; Barnabas 9:1–9; Barnabas 15:1–9; Barnabas 18:1–20:2; Romans 9:4–5; Romans 11:28–29

sections.b: An anonymous sermon, read aloud in worship 'after the God of truth', that is, after the Scripture (2 Clement 19:1). Lake calls it 'a letter only in form' and dates it 'between 120 and 170 A.D.', most often about 150; Lightfoot called it 'the first example of a Christian homily'. Its hearers were Gentile converts who had worshiped idols (1:6). It quotes many sayings of Jesus, some in no Gospel (4:5; 5:2-4; 12:2, which Clement of Alexandria found in the Gospel of the Egyptians), and calls a Gospel saying 'Scripture' (2:4). It bears Clement's name only because it was copied after 1 Clement; Eusebius said the ancients made no use of it (Church History 3.38.4), and Lake that 'it cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement'.

The longest of Ignatius's seven letters, written from Smyrna about the reign of Trajan to the church of Ephesus, which had sent its overseer Onesimus to meet him (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3). It presses unity with 'the overseer and the council of elders' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:2) in the picture of a choir, confesses Christ as 'God in man' against those who said he only seemed to suffer (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2), and calls the church's one bread 'the medicine of immortality' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2). Lightfoot called Ignatius 'the staunchest advocate of episcopacy in the early ages'. See the topic Ignatius of Antioch.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2

sections.b: Written from Smyrna and dated 24 August in Lake's rendering (10:3), the letter asks the Roman church not to save Ignatius from the beasts: 'I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found pure bread of Christ' (4:1); 'Now I am beginning to be a disciple' (5:3). Lake: it 'has the object of preventing the Christians at Rome from making any efforts to save Ignatius'. The churches read its greeting, to the church that 'presides in the region of the Romans' and is 'presiding over the love' (1:0), in different ways. Irenaeus quotes it about AD 180 (Against Heresies 5.28.4).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 1:0; Ignatius to the Romans 4:1; Ignatius to the Romans 5:3; Ignatius to the Romans 10:3

sections.b: Written from Troas to the church at Smyrna against those who said Christ 'suffered only in appearance' (2:1). It confesses him 'truly born of a virgin' and 'truly nailed' under Pontius Pilate and Herod (1:1-2), says the thanksgiving 'is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ' (7:1), and has the phrase 'the catholic church' (8:2), which the Catholic Encyclopedia calls its first use. A fifth-century papyrus at Berlin holds 3:3-12:1 (Lake).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:2

sections.h: The other four letters of Ignatius
sections.b: To the Magnesians and To the Trallians were written from Smyrna, after the overseers of the two churches came to meet the prisoner there (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.5); To the Philadelphians and To Polycarp were written from Troas (3.36). To the Magnesians warns against living 'by Judaism' and has the earliest known use of the word 'Christianity' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:1-3); To the Trallians says of overseer, elders and deacons, 'Without these, it is not called a church' (Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1); To the Philadelphians answers those who would believe nothing they could not find 'in the archives' (Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2); To Polycarp is the only one of the seven written to one person. See the topic Ignatius of Antioch.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:1-3; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 8:2; Ignatius to Polycarp 1:0

sections.b: An anonymous defense of the faith addressed to 'most excellent Diognetus' (Epistle to Diognetus 1:1), with its picture of Christians as resident aliens and citizens of heaven (5:5, 9) and 'the sweet exchange' (9:5). Lake says its place among the Apostolic Fathers 'rests on custom rather than right, for it is probably later than any of the other writings in this group'; the Catholic Encyclopedia (Chapman, 1909) says it was classed with them 'since the eighteenth century' through 'a misunderstanding' of the words 'disciple of apostles' (11:1), which belong to a separate homily joined to it (chapters 11-12). It survived in one manuscript, burned at Strasburg in 1870.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 1:1; Epistle to Diognetus 5:5; Epistle to Diognetus 9:5; Epistle to Diognetus 11:1

sections.b: The longest of these writings, a Roman book of five Visions, twelve Mandates and ten Similitudes, told by Hermas, who says the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda in Rome. Its message is that Christians who have sinned after baptism may still repent, once (Shepherd of Hermas 6:4–5; Shepherd of Hermas 31:6); its pictures are the Church as an old woman, the tower built of stones, and the rock and the gate that are the Son of God (Shepherd of Hermas 89:1–6). The Muratorian Fragment dates it to the time of Hermas's brother Pius, bishop of Rome (Lake: about 148), though the Fragment's own date is disputed. Eusebius read Irenaeus as receiving it as Scripture (Church History 5.8.7) and Codex Sinaiticus copies it after the New Testament (Chapman, 1910), but the Muratorian Fragment and Athanasius kept it for reading outside the canon, and Eusebius put it among the spurious books. See the topics Hermas and Penance: Forgiveness after Baptism.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 6:4–5; Shepherd of Hermas 8:1; Shepherd of Hermas 31:6; Shepherd of Hermas 89:1–6
